text: inhalational anaesthetic nitrous oxide, given with oxy- gen, is suitable for self-administration and is commonly used to relieve labour pain. It is relatively safe and can pro- duce substantial analgesia in most patients.6 Other inhala- tional analgesics such as isoflurane or sevoflurane are also sometimes used7 (see Choice of Analgesic, above). Opioid analgesics have been given systemically in the management of labour pain for many years, although they do not appear to provide adequate analgesia in most pa- tients at a tolerable dosage.8,9 There is no clear evidence to favour one opioid over another.10 Morphine is considered unsuitable,7 and the widest experience has been with pethi- dine.7,10 However, its effectiveness has been queried,7,10 and its use has declined in many countries.7 Fentanyl and its derivatives sufentanil and alfentanil have been used, particularly when given as intravenous patient-controlled analgesia,7 but it is not clear that they have any great ad- vantages, and as with other opioids they may cross the pla- centa and produce respiratory depression and other ad- verse effects in the newborn. The use of the very short- acting opioid remifentanil for patient-controlled analgesia during labour has been investigated, with some benefit,11 but although it is less likely to produce effects on neonatal respiration it is not clear that the degree of supervision re- quired to guard against unacceptable respiratory depres- sion in the mother can be widely achieved on busy labour wards.7 Nalbuphine has been used in some countries be- cause of its mixed agonist/antagonist action,7 although there does not seem to be clear evidence that it conveys any substantial benefit. Epidural analgesia with a local anaesthetic is now con- sidered the gold standard for treatment and provides the most effective pain relief during labour.9,12-14 Medical in- dications may include a history of malignant hyperther- mia, certain cardiovascular or respiratory disorders, or pre- eclampsia, but the primary indication is the patient’s desire for pain relief.9,13 Bupivacaine is one of the local anaes- thetics most often used in epidural analgesia; others in- clude ropivacaine and lidocaine.14 Epidural block has few contra-indications and serious ad- verse events are rare. Nonetheless, it has been associated with an increased risk of prolonged second-stage labour, forceps delivery, and caesarean section9,13,14 (although meta-analysis8 and a systematic review14 refute the latter), and it may not improve maternal experience of childbirth.
